evidence: On March 31, 2025, Inclusiv, Inc., a 50-year-old nonprofit organization that partners with credit unions to promote financial security, filed suit against the Environmental Protection Agency, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, Acting Deputy Administrator W.C. McIntosh, and Citibank, N.A.
The nonprofit is represented by private counsel from Venable LLP.

The case was assigned to Judge Tanya S. Chutkan and was later consolidated with Case No. 25-cv-698 on April 15, 2025, along with several other related cases involving other Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grant recipients.

Inclusiv challenges EPA's freeze and attempted termination of its $1.87 billion grant under the Clean Communities Investment Accelerator program, part of the nearly $27 billion Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund established by Congress in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

Inclusiv brings claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging EPA's actions violate the Inflation Reduction Act, the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act, the Anti-Deficiency Act, and EPA's own regulations at 2 C.F.R. §§ 200.339-342.

The nonprofit also asserts constitutional violations under the Separation of Powers doctrine (specifically the Legislative Vesting Clause, Spending and Appropriations Clauses, and Take Care Clause) and the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
Against Citibank, which serves as the financial agent holding the grant funds, Inclusiv brings state law claims for breach of contract, conversion, and replevin.
Inclusiv seeks declaratory judgment and injunctive relief.
EPA competitively awarded Inclusiv the grant in April 2024, with a formal grant agreement executed on August 8, 2024, for a performance period running through June 30, 2030.
The funds were deposited into an account at Citibank pursuant to a Financial Agency Agreement between Citibank and Treasury and an Account Control Agreement among Inclusiv, Citibank, and EPA.

By February 2025, Inclusiv had selected 108 credit union subrecipients across 27 states and Puerto Rico to receive $651 million in subawards for clean energy projects in low- and moderate-income communities.
On February 12, 2025, EPA Administrator Zeldin publicly announced EPA's intention to "return the entire fund balance to the U.S. Treasury," calling the program "criminal."
Since mid-February 2025, Inclusiv has been unable to access its funds, as Citibank refused to process disbursement requests despite its ministerial obligations under the Account Control Agreement.

On March 11, 2025, Acting Deputy Administrator McIntosh sent termination letters to all GGRF grant recipients, citing unspecified concerns about "program integrity," "fraud, waste, and abuse," and "misalignment with the Agency's priorities."
The termination letter did not provide Inclusiv any opportunity to respond or challenge the decision.

Inclusiv filed a motion for preliminary injunction on April 1, 2025, and initially filed an emergency motion for temporary restraining order the same day after discovering its account balance had dropped to zero.
The nonprofit withdrew the TRO request on April 2, 2025, after receiving assurances that the funds had been moved into a money market account as part of a monthly process.
The Court stayed briefing on the preliminary injunction motion on April 10, 2025, pending resolution of related matters in the consolidated lead case.
On April 16, 2025, the Court denied Inclusiv's preliminary injunction motion as moot, referring to a preliminary injunction order issued in the lead case.

EPA awarded the grant in April 2024, with a formal grant agreement on August 8, 2024, for a performance period running through June 30, 2030, and deposited the funds at Citibank pursuant to a Financial Agency Agreement and Account Control Agreement; by February 2025, Inclusiv had selected 108 credit union subrecipients across 27 states and Puerto Rico to receive $651 million in subawards for clean energy projects in low- and moderate-income communities. On February 12, 2025, Administrator Zeldin announced intent to return the entire fund balance to Treasury and called the program criminal. evidence: On April 11, 2025, five F-1 visa holders - three current students and two post-graduate Optional Practical Training (OPT) workers in the Northern District of California - filed suit against Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, ICE Acting Director Todd M. Lyons, San Francisco ICE Acting Field Office Director Moises Becerra, and President Donald J. Trump in their official capacities. The plaintiffs, proceeding under pseudonyms S.Y., Z.D., Y.W., H.G., and W.X., are represented by private counsel from Van Der Hout LLP.

The case arose from a widespread pattern beginning April 4, 2025, in which ICE's Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) terminated the Student and Exchange Visitor Information Systems (SEVIS) records of hundreds of F-1 students nationwide. Between April 4 and April 8, 2025, each plaintiff received notice that their SEVIS record had been terminated with the reason listed as "Otherwise Failing to Maintain Status – Individual identified in criminal records check and/or has had their visa revoked." Three plaintiffs also received notices from the State Department that their F-1 visas had been revoked.

The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and the Declaratory Judgment Act, alleging that the SEVIS terminations were unauthorized, arbitrary and capricious, and violated due process under the Fifth Amendment. They argued that none of them had violated their F-1 status requirements - two plaintiffs had minor misdemeanor convictions that were not crimes of violence, two had arrests without convictions, and one had a prior deportation for which they had received a waiver and subsequently been granted a new visa. The plaintiffs contended that under federal regulations, these circumstances did not constitute grounds for terminating their SEVIS records or F-1 status.

The plaintiffs sought declaratory and injunctive relief to prevent enforcement actions, arrest, detention, transfer, or removal based on the SEVIS terminations. They argued that terminating SEVIS records effectively strips students of their ability to continue their studies or OPT employment, as the DHS website indicates that SEVIS termination results in loss of employment authorization and triggers potential ICE enforcement action.

The case was initially assigned to Judge Noel Wise but was reassigned to Judge Jeffrey S. White on April 22, 2025, after being found related to another case, Doe v. Trump. On April 17, 2025, Judge Wise granted the plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order, finding they had shown serious questions on the merits and likelihood of irreparable harm. The TRO enjoined defendants from arresting, incarcerating, or transferring the plaintiffs and from imposing any legal effect from the SEVIS terminations. This TRO was extended by Judge White on April 25, 2025.

Following briefing and hearings, Judge White granted the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction on May 22, 2025, maintaining the same protections. The court found that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their APA claims that the SEVIS terminations were not in compliance with federal regulations and were arbitrary and capricious. The government filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on July 21, 2025 (Case No. 25-4523) and subsequently moved to stay the injunction pending appeal on August 8, 2025.

The case highlighted a broader pattern of SEVIS terminations affecting international students at universities across California and the nation, including the University of California system and Stanford University, creating significant uncertainty for schools and students about the basis and consequences of these administrative actions.

The court granted a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, enjoining enforcement based on the SEVIS terminations. The government appealed and sought a stay. The case reflects a nationwide pattern of SEVIS terminations affecting students at major universities.

evidence: On May 17, 2025, Darwin Antonio Arevalo Millan, a Venezuelan citizen detained at the Desert View Annex facility associated with the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, filed a habeas corpus petition and class action complaint challenging his detention and potential removal under Presidential Proclamation No. 10903.

The Proclamation, issued on March 14, 2025, invoked the Alien Enemies Act (50 U.S.C. §§ 21 et seq.) for only the fourth time in U.S. history, authorizing the immediate detention and removal of Venezuelan nationals allegedly affiliated with Tren de Aragua, which the President designated as a foreign terrorist organization conducting "irregular warfare" against the United States.

The petitioner, an asylum applicant who had previously been granted parole to work and reside in the United States pending his asylum proceedings, was arrested during a routine ICE check‑in without prior notice or documentation of the arrest basis.
He was allegedly told his detention related to his Venezuelan nationality and tattoos that might indicate gang affiliation, though he maintained they were basketball‑related.

Judge John W. Holcomb granted a temporary restraining order on May 19, 2025, and certified a class for limited purposes consisting of all noncitizens in custody in the Central District of California subject to the Proclamation.

Following a hearing on May 30, 2025, the court issued a preliminary injunction on June 2, 2025, enjoining the government from removing or transferring class members out of the district under the Alien Enemies Act pending further court order regarding adequate notice requirements.

The court found the petitioner likely to succeed on his due process claims, noting that detainees subject to removal under the Alien Enemies Act are entitled to notice and opportunity to challenge their removal, as established by the Supreme Court's decisions in Trump v. J.G.G. and A.A.R.P. v. Trump.

A dispute arose regarding the basis for the petitioner's continued detention after he was granted asylum on June 9, 2025. The petitioner filed an emergency application for habeas corpus on June 14, 2025, seeking immediate release, but the court denied it on June 20, 2025, finding the government could detain him pending appeal of the asylum grant under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A).
The government filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on August 1, 2025, challenging the preliminary injunction order, with the appeal assigned docket number 25‑4866.

evidence: On May 22, 2025, Shira Perlmutter, the Register of Copyrights and Director of the U.S. Copyright Office, filed suit challenging her purported removal by President Donald J. Trump.
The case arose after President Trump fired Librarian of Congress Carla D. Hayden on May 8, 2025, reportedly over concerns about diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.
Two days later, on May 10, the White House Presidential Personnel Office, through Deputy Director Trent Morse, terminated Perlmutter's position "effective immediately."
The timing followed one day after the Copyright Office issued a pre-publication report on copyright and artificial intelligence.

President Trump then purported to appoint Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche as acting Librarian of Congress without Senate confirmation, and Blanche designated Associate Deputy Attorney General Paul Perkins as acting Register of Copyrights.
When Justice Department officials attempted to access the Library of Congress on May 12 to assume these positions, Library staff contacted the U.S. Capitol Police, and the officials left voluntarily.

Perlmutter, represented by the Democracy Forward Foundation and the law firm Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP, sued President Trump in his official capacity, Blanche, Perkins, the White House Presidential Personnel officials (Sergio Gor and Trent Morse), and the Executive Office of the President.
She brought two ultra vires claims arguing that the President's actions violated both constitutional and statutory authority.

First, she contended that the President cannot appoint an acting Librarian of Congress because the Library is not an "Executive agency" under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (5 U.S.C. § 3345), and therefore the President lacks authority to make temporary appointments there.

Second, she argued that her removal violated the Appointments Clause and separation of powers principles because Congress vested the appointment and removal power for the Register of Copyrights exclusively in the Librarian of Congress under 17 U.S.C. § 701(a), not in the President.
Perlmutter sought declaratory and injunctive relief to prevent her removal and the defendants from exercising the powers of their claimed positions.
She immediately moved for a temporary restraining order on May 22, which Judge Timothy J. Kelly denied on May 28, 2025, finding she had not established irreparable harm.
She then filed a motion for preliminary injunction on June 10, which the court similarly denied on July 30, 2025.

In a detailed memorandum opinion, Judge Kelly concluded that Perlmutter failed to demonstrate the "genuinely extraordinary situation" required under Sampson v. Murray for preliminary relief in government personnel cases.
Following the denial of her preliminary injunction motion, Perlmutter filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit on July 31, 2025, and moved for an injunction pending appeal on August 4.
Judge Kelly denied this motion as well on August 20, 2025, reiterating that she had not shown irreparable harm.
The case remains pending with cross-motions for summary judgment scheduled for hearing on November 4, 2025, while the appeal proceeds in the D.C. Circuit under case number 25-5285.

The court denied her temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction for lack of irreparable harm, and the case remains pending with summary‑judgment motions set for November 4, 2025, under case number 25‑5285.

evidence: On May 10, 2016, seven current and former residents of the Alexander County Housing Authority filed a class action lawsuit against the housing authority and its current and former executive directors, alleging rampant racial discrimination and family status discrimination at the McBride and Elmwood public housing developments in Cairo, Illinois. The plaintiffs, represented by the Hughes Socol law firm and the Sargent Shriver National Center on Poverty Law, brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Illinois Civil Rights Act of 2003. They sought declaratory judgment, injunctive relief, and monetary damages.

The plaintiffs alleged that ACHA engaged in a pattern and practice of segregating its public housing developments by race, with approximately 97% of McBride and Elmwood residents being African-American, while white households predominated in other ACHA developments including Connell Smith. This occurred despite African-Americans comprising only 36% of Alexander County's population and despite a 1974 Department of Justice lawsuit that had previously addressed ACHA's racial segregation.

The complaint detailed severe maintenance failures at the predominantly African-American developments, including infestations of mice, roaches, and bedbugs; mold; and serious plumbing, heating, and electrical deficiencies, while the Connell Smith development was adequately maintained with security cameras and guards.
The plaintiffs also alleged that ACHA prohibited families with children from living in certain developments to prevent African-American families from living in majority-white buildings.

Supporting these allegations, on September 30, 2014, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development had issued findings that ACHA violated Title VI through intentional racial segregation at McBride and Elmwood, and HUD ultimately took over ACHA's operations in February 2016.

The plaintiffs filed three amended complaints between July 2016 and February 2017, ultimately expanding to 35 named plaintiffs while dropping initial rent overcharge claims to focus on the discrimination claims and adding state law claims for breach of residential leases, negligence, and willful and wanton conduct.

The defendants were narrowed to ACHA, James Wilson (Executive Director from 1989-2013), and Martha Franklin (Executive Director from April 2013-January 2015), with defendants Thomas Upchurch and Joanne Pink voluntarily dismissed in September 2016 and January 2017.

Settlement negotiations began in earnest in 2017, with multiple settlement conferences held before Magistrate Judge Daly between February and June 2017. During this period, counsel withdrew from representing three plaintiffs (LaTonya Lee, Denieshia Childress, and Coretta Cornelius) in April and May 2017 after being unable to maintain contact with them.

On July 27, 2017, the represented plaintiffs filed a stipulation dismissing their claims against all defendants with prejudice and without costs, with each party bearing its own attorneys' fees. The three unrepresented plaintiffs failed to respond to court orders about proceeding with their claims, and on September 12, 2017, Chief Judge Reagan dismissed their claims for failure to prosecute and approved the voluntary dismissal of the represented plaintiffs' claims, closing the case without trial.
The case was assigned to Chief Judge Michael J. Reagan with referral to Magistrate Judge Reona J. Daly.

They alleged that the ACHA engaged in a pattern of segregating its developments by race, with McBride and Elmwood being approximately 97% African‑American while other ACHA developments were predominantly white, despite the county’s 36% African‑American population and a prior 1974 DOJ lawsuit. The complaint documented severe maintenance failures at McBride and Elmwood—infestations of mice, roaches, bedbugs, mold, and serious plumbing, heating, and electrical deficiencies—contrasted with adequate maintenance, security cameras, and guards at Connell Smith. They also alleged that the ACHA prohibited families with children from living in certain developments to keep African‑American families out of majority‑white buildings. The United States Supreme Court subsequently found this removal improper in Noem v. Abrego Garcia, 145 S. Ct. 1017 (2025), and ordered the government to facilitate his return.

evidence: The government immediately sought pretrial detention, arguing that the offenses involved minor victims under 18 U.S.C. § 3142(f)(1)(E), that Abrego posed a serious flight risk, and that he presented a danger to the community. The government's case relied heavily on testimony from Homeland Security Agent Peter Joseph, who recounted statements from cooperating witnesses—including two men who were themselves involved in the alleged smuggling conspiracy and were closely related family members. These cooperators claimed Abrego transported undocumented individuals for payment of $1,000-$1,500 per trip as part of a smuggling business called "Trans Express", and that he sometimes transported minors and brought his own children on smuggling trips. The government also presented evidence from the November 2022 traffic stop, including a handwritten roster suggesting one passenger might have been a minor, though the handwriting was ambiguous and could have indicated either a 2001 or 2007 birth year.

evidence: Magistrate Judge Barbara D. Holmes held extensive hearings on June 13, 2025, and issued a detailed 51-page opinion on June 22, 2025, denying the government's detention motion. The court found the government failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of evidence that the case involved minor victims, noting significant reliability problems with the cooperating witnesses' testimony—including their substantial incentives to cooperate (early release from prison, deferred deportation) and evolving statements that grew more incriminating over time. The court also found insufficient evidence of flight risk or danger to the community.

After additional briefing and an evidentiary hearing on July 16, 2025, where Agent Joseph provided supplemental testimony, Judge Crenshaw issued a 37-page opinion on July 23, 2025. While finding the government had shown by a preponderance that the crimes involved minor victims (entitling it to a detention hearing), the court agreed with the magistrate judge that the government failed to establish by clear and convincing evidence that Abrego posed such a danger that no conditions could ensure community safety, or by a preponderance that he was likely to flee.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I reviewed the summary, identified the lawsuit details, the rule challenged, the plaintiffs’ legal basis, the court’s findings, and the background context, and extracted these as the factual basis.

evidence: On July 1, 2025, three city governments (Columbus, Baltimore, and Chicago), along with Doctors for America (a nonprofit organization of over 27,000 physicians and medical trainees) and Main Street Alliance (a network of approximately 30,000 small businesses), filed suit against Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in his capacity as Secretary of Health and Human Services, HHS, Mehmet Oz as CMS Administrator, and CMS.

The plaintiffs, represented by Democracy Forward Foundation, challenged the "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Rule" published on June 25, 2025, which was set to take effect on August 25, 2025.
The plaintiffs brought their challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing that multiple provisions of the Rule were both contrary to law and arbitrary and capricious.
CMS acknowledged that the Rule would cause at least 1.8 million Americans to lose health coverage in 2026 alone.

On July 2, 2025, the plaintiffs filed a motion seeking a stay under 5 U.S.C. § 705 or, alternatively, a preliminary injunction to prevent the Rule from taking effect. They challenged nine specific provisions, including: a $5 monthly surcharge on certain low-income enrollees who are automatically re-enrolled; changes to premium adjustment methodology that would increase out-of-pocket costs; expansion of permitted actuarial value variations that would reduce plan coverage; allowing insurers to deny coverage to applicants with past-due premiums; reinstating a one-year failure-to-reconcile tax credit penalty; and various income verification requirements that would create barriers to enrollment.
The court found that the plaintiffs had standing based on increased costs and uncompensated care they would face from increased uninsured populations.

The court stayed the effective date of the seven challenged provisions it found likely unlawful, determining that plaintiffs would suffer irreparable harm from implementation including small businesses being forced to close and cities bearing increased uncompensated care costs.

The case represents a continuation of litigation over ACA implementation, with Judge Hurson noting that similar challenges to similar provisions had been brought successfully by some of the same city plaintiffs in City of Columbus v. Cochran in 2021, where Judge Chasanow had vacated comparable income verification requirements as arbitrary and capricious.
The stay applies nationwide pending final resolution on the merits, with the court rejecting the government's request to limit relief only to the plaintiffs.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed on July 1, 2025 by the cities of Columbus, Baltimore, and Chicago, Doctors for America, and Main Street Alliance, challenging the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Rule published June 25, 2025 and set to take effect August 25, 2025; the plaintiffs alleged that nine provisions were contrary to law and arbitrary/capricious and sought a stay or preliminary injunction. The court found standing and likely success on seven of nine challenges, and stayed those seven provisions nationwide pending final resolution on the merits, citing potential irreparable harm including small businesses being forced to close and cities bearing increased uncompensated care costs. The Rule was estimated to cause at least 1.8 million Americans to lose coverage in 2026, and the case builds on prior litigation such as City of Columbus v. Cochran (2021).

The Order further prohibits local public radio stations from using federal funds to acquire NPR programming, requiring CPB to revise its eligibility criteria to implement these restrictions by June 30, 2025.

The accompanying White House fact sheet characterized NPR's content as 'left-wing propaganda' and criticized specific editorial decisions, including coverage of COVID-19 origins and the Hunter Biden laptop story.

The plaintiffs assert equitable causes of action seeking declaratory and injunctive relief based on violations of the First Amendment's prohibitions against viewpoint discrimination and retaliation, the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause, and multiple federal statutes.

Most significantly, they argue the Order violates the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, which expressly prohibits 'any department, agency, officer, or employee of the United States' from exercising 'any direction, supervision, or control' over CPB or its grantees.

The Act requires CPB to distribute funds based on neutral criteria and designates NPR as the entity managing the Public Radio Satellite System, which serves 379 stations and enables emergency alerts to reach 99 percent of Americans.

NPR produces and distributes programming to 246 independent member stations nationwide, receiving approximately $100 million annually (31 percent of its operating revenue) through membership and licensing fees from these stations.

The local member station plaintiffs—Aspen Public Radio, Colorado Public Radio, and KSUT Public Radio—each receive CPB Community Service Grants ranging from $210,000 to $1.4 million annually, representing between 6 and 19 percent of their budgets.
Under statutory requirements, a portion of these grants must be used to acquire nationally distributed programming.
Following the Order's issuance, the National Endowment for the Arts terminated two grants to NPR effective May 31, 2025, though both grants had been fully paid in February 2025.
CPB issued a public statement asserting it would not comply with the Order, maintaining that as a private corporation it is not subject to presidential authority.
In response, the Administration has attempted to remove three of CPB's five board members, leading to separate litigation (CPB v. Trump, No. 25-cv-1305).
On July 14, 2025, CPB issued a Request for Proposals seeking a new entity to replace NPR as manager of the Public Radio Satellite System.
Both parties filed motions for summary judgment, with plaintiffs filing on June 13, 2025, and federal defendants filing a cross-motion on July 12, 2025.
The federal defendants argue primarily that the claims are not ripe because CPB has not yet terminated funding, and that the government has broad discretion in making funding decisions.

Plaintiffs counter that they are already suffering First Amendment injuries from the Order's chilling effect on their speech and that the Order clearly violates both statutory prohibitions and constitutional protections against viewpoint-based discrimination and retaliation for protected speech.

Additionally, Congress recently enacted the President's rescission request eliminating CPB funding for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, though funding for fiscal year 2025 and satellite interconnection purposes remains.
The case remains pending before Judge Moss.

evidence: On July 21, 2025, twenty-three nonprofit organizations filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island challenging new conditions that the Departments of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and Health and Human Services (HHS) imposed on federal grant programs.
The case arose from a series of executive orders issued by President Trump in January 2025 targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs, transgender rights, and abortion access.

The HUD conditions, applied to Continuum of Care grants and other programs administered by the Office of Community Planning and Development, prohibit recipients from using grant funds to promote "gender ideology", require certification that recipients do not operate programs violating federal antidiscrimination laws, prohibit funding or promoting "elective abortions", and mandate compliance with all current executive orders.

The HHS conditions, incorporated through revised grant policy statements and standard terms, require recipients to certify they do not operate programs that advance or promote DEI, DEIA (diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility), or "discriminatory equity ideology" in violation of federal anti-discrimination laws.

The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act alleging that the agencies exceeded their statutory authority, acted contrary to law, failed to follow required procedures, and acted arbitrarily and capriciously.

They also raised constitutional claims under the First Amendment (arguing the conditions restrict protected speech and compel government-approved viewpoints), the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause (arguing the conditions are unconstitutionally vague), the Spending Clause, and separation of powers principles.

The complaint emphasizes that the new conditions conflict with existing statutory requirements, particularly those directing grant recipients to serve underserved populations including racial and ethnic minorities and LGBTQ+ individuals, and with existing regulations requiring grantees to treat individuals according to their gender identity.

The plaintiffs argue these conditions place them in an impossible position: either accept the conditions and risk False Claims Act liability while abandoning core aspects of their missions, or refuse the funding and cease critical services to domestic violence survivors, sexual assault victims, and homeless individuals.

The complaint details how the administration explicitly plans to use the False Claims Act as a "weapon" against organizations that engage in disfavored DEI activities, with Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche announcing a "Civil Rights Fraud Initiative" targeting federal funding recipients.
On July 24, 2025, Judge Melissa R. DuBose held a hearing on the plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order.

On July 28, the court granted the TRO, enjoining HUD from enforcing the challenged conditions on Continuum of Care grants for certain plaintiffs and enjoining HHS from enforcing the anti-DEI certification requirement on Family Violence Prevention Services Act State Domestic Violence Coalition grants for certain plaintiffs.
The court found that plaintiffs demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits and would suffer immediate and irreparable harm without relief.
The TRO has been amended several times to include additional plaintiffs and grant programs, most recently on August 20, 2025, to include Community Development Block Grants.
The defendants filed notices of compliance with the TRO, and the parties have briefed a motion for preliminary injunction scheduled for hearing on September 4, 2025.
The plaintiffs seek to stay the challenged policies under 5 U.S.C. § 705 and to preliminarily enjoin enforcement of all the new conditions pending resolution of the case.
The case remains in active litigation with no settlement discussions reported.

The plaintiffs are represented by a coalition of legal organizations including the ACLU Foundation of Rhode Island, the Lawyers' Committee for Rhode Island, Democracy Forward Foundation, the National Women's Law Center, and private counsel.

evidence: On April 9, 2025, the Southern Education Foundation (SEF), represented by private counsel, filed suit against the U.S. Department of Education, Secretary Linda McMahon in her official capacity, and President Donald J. Trump in his official capacity, challenging the termination of a federal grant.

In October 2022, the Department of Education awarded SEF a five-year, $8.6 million grant to operate the Equity Assistance Center for the southern region (EAC-South) under Title IV of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which authorizes technical assistance for public school desegregation.
On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14151 directing federal agencies to terminate "equity-related" grants and programs.

On February 13, 2025, the Department sent SEF a termination letter stating that the grant "provides funding for programs that promote or take part in DEI initiatives" that allegedly violate federal civil rights laws.
The termination was immediate and without prior notice or opportunity to respond.
While the letter offered an administrative appeal process, SEF withdrew its appeal on May 16, 2025.

SEF brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act alleging the termination was arbitrary and capricious and violated required procedures, as well as claims under the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause (vagueness), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the First Amendment (viewpoint discrimination), and ultra vires impoundment of congressionally appropriated funds.
SEF sought declaratory judgment and injunctive relief to reinstate the grant.
On April 23, 2025, SEF filed a motion for a preliminary injunction.

After oral argument on May 12, 2025, Judge Friedman granted the preliminary injunction on May 21, 2025, finding SEF was likely to succeed on the merits of its APA claim that the termination was arbitrary and capricious.

The court found the Department provided no reasoned explanation for the termination, conducted no individualized assessment of EAC-South's programming, and failed to articulate any rational connection between facts found and the termination decision.
The court also found SEF would suffer irreparable harm from loss of funding that threatened EAC-South's existence and ability to assist school districts with desegregation compliance.
The court ordered the Department to reinstate the grant within five business days.
On July 18, 2025, the defendants filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, where the case is docketed as No. 25-5262.

The School District sought declaratory judgment and injunctive relief based on violations of the First Amendment's free speech protections, the Fifth Amendment's due process clause, the Spending Clause, and the Administrative Procedure Act, as well as ultra vires claims.

The case arose from the School District's receipt of a $6 million federal mental health grant distributed over five years under the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which Congress passed in 2022 following the Uvalde school shooting to expand mental health services in schools.
The Act appropriated $1 billion over five years for mental health supports in schools.
After taking office, President Trump issued multiple executive orders targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs.

On February 14, 2025, the Department of Education issued a Dear Colleague Letter threatening schools with loss of federal funding if they continued DEI programs, though the letter failed to define key terms like "diversity," "equity," or "inclusion."
The Department also established an "End DEI" complaint portal for reporting alleged discrimination in schools.

On April 29, 2025, the Department issued a Notice of Non-Continuation of Grant Award to the School District, stating the mental health programs violated federal civil rights law, conflicted with the Department's priorities of merit and excellence in education, undermined student well-being, or constituted inappropriate use of federal funds.
The School District had already received $3,605,500 of the grant through December 2025 and was entitled to an additional $2,394,500 through 2027.

The grant funding had enabled the School District to hire seven additional mental health professionals, establish wellness rooms that served 830 students (40% of enrollment), reduce bullying reports by 30%, decrease disruptive behavior incidents, and provide 24/7 mental health support through a mobile app.
The School District did not seek administrative reconsideration of the non-continuation decision.
The School District filed a motion for temporary restraining order and/or preliminary injunction on June 23, 2025.

Judge William P. Johnson of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico held a hearing on July 16, 2025, where the School District presented witness testimony about the irreparable harm from loss of funding.
On July 18, 2025, Judge Johnson denied the motion for preliminary injunction and dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of jurisdiction.
The court concluded that the dispute was essentially a contract claim over grant funding that belonged in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act, not in district court.
The court found that even though the School District framed its claims as constitutional and statutory violations, the essence of the suit was seeking payment of grant money.

The court also found the School District unlikely to succeed on the merits of its First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Spending Clause, ultra vires, and APA claims, and that irreparable harm was not established since money damages could remedy any injury.

evidence: On April 4, 2025, the Association for Education Finance and Policy, Inc. (a nonprofit membership organization of education scholars and practitioners) and the Institute for Higher Education Policy (a nonprofit research organization focused on postsecondary education access) filed suit against Secretary of Education Linda McMahon and the U.S. Department of Education.

On February 10, 2025, the Department began canceling numerous IES contracts, terminating studies including the 2020/25 Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study, the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009, the High School and Beyond Longitudinal Study of 2022, and the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study-Kindergarten 2024. The Department also terminated IES's peer review program for new grant funding and halted processing of applications for access to restricted-use research data. On March 11, 2025, Secretary McMahon announced a reduction-in-force affecting approximately 90% of IES staff positions.

The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), alleging the terminations were contrary to law and arbitrary and capricious. They argued that the Department violated multiple statutory provisions requiring IES to conduct specific research activities and disseminate data. The Institute for Higher Education Policy also alleged unreasonable delay in processing its pending requests for disclosure risk review of research using restricted-use data.

The underlying facts show that the challenged programs involved long-term longitudinal studies tracking students from early childhood through postsecondary education, with some studies having collected data for multiple years before termination. The plaintiffs and their members rely on this data for research, policy analysis, and publications related to education finance and policy. The terminations occurred without consultation with stakeholders and, according to the plaintiffs, will result in the loss of data already collected and waste of millions in appropriated funds.

evidence: On March 31, 2025, three groups of civil rights and political organizations filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging Executive Order 14,248, issued by President Trump on March 25, 2025.

The plaintiffs include the League of United Latin American Citizens, Secure Families Initiative, and Arizona Students' Association (the "LULAC Plaintiffs"), represented by the Campaign Legal Center and State Democracy Defenders Fund; the League of Women Voters and several other voting rights organizations (the "League Plaintiffs"), represented by the ACLU and other counsel; and the Democratic National Committee, other Democratic Party organizations, and congressional leaders Charles Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries (the "Democratic Party Plaintiffs"), represented by private counsel.
The plaintiffs brought ultra vires claims alleging that the President exceeded his constitutional and statutory authority by attempting to unilaterally regulate federal elections.

They argued that the Executive Order violated the separation of powers by usurping authority that the Constitution's Elections Clause (Article I, Section 4) reserves to Congress and the States, not the President.

The challenged provisions included Section 2(a), which directed the Election Assistance Commission (EAC) to require documentary proof of citizenship on the federal voter registration form; Section 2(d), which ordered federal agencies to assess citizenship before providing voter registration forms to public assistance recipients; Section 2(b), which directed agencies to share databases to identify non-citizen voters; and Sections 7(a) and 7(b), which directed enforcement of ballot receipt deadlines.
The plaintiffs sought declaratory judgment and injunctive relief to prevent implementation of these provisions.

The plaintiffs filed motions for preliminary injunction on April 7, 2025, arguing that the Executive Order would make it more difficult for eligible citizens to register to vote, particularly those lacking passports or other specified documents.

Many of the plaintiff organizations conduct voter registration drives and provide registration assistance, while the Democratic Party Plaintiffs asserted competitive harm to their electoral prospects.

The organizations demonstrated that many eligible voters, including students, military families, and naturalized citizens, often lack easy access to the narrow forms of documentary proof specified in the Executive Order.
After briefing and a hearing on April 17, 2025, Judge Kollar-Kotelly issued her decision on April 24, 2025.
The court granted preliminary injunctive relief as to Sections 2(a) and 2(d), finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of their separation-of-powers claims.

The court held that neither the Constitution nor any statute grants the President authority to dictate the contents of the federal voter registration form or to direct agencies to assess citizenship before providing registration forms, as these powers belong to Congress and the States.

The court emphasized that while Congress was currently debating legislation that would implement similar requirements through the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, the President could not short-circuit the legislative process by executive order.
The court denied relief as to Sections 2(b), 7(a), and 7(b), finding those challenges either premature or more properly brought by the States themselves.
The court noted that several states had already filed separate challenges to these provisions in Massachusetts and Washington federal courts.

The preliminary injunction prohibits the EAC and its officials from modifying the federal voter registration form to require documentary proof of citizenship, and prohibits the Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs, Department of Interior, and Small Business Administration from implementing the citizenship assessment requirement for public assistance recipients.
The Republican National Committee successfully moved to intervene as a defendant on June 12, 2025.
Discovery and summary judgment briefing are currently underway, with the parties filing cross-motions for partial summary judgment on the Section 2(a) claims in July and August 2025.

The court did not require the plaintiffs to post an injunction bond, finding that the defendants had not shown they would suffer material harm from the preliminary injunction and that requiring a bond might deter legitimate challenges to executive action.

evidence: On May 29, 2025, eleven Roman Catholic clergy members—including the Archbishop of Seattle, the Bishops of Yakima and Spokane, and several priests from those dioceses—filed suit in federal court challenging Washington Senate Bill 5375 on First and Fourteenth Amendment grounds.

The case centers on SB 5375, signed into law on May 2, 2025 and set to take effect July 27, 2025, which adds clergy to Washington's list of mandatory reporters for child abuse and neglect while explicitly removing their ability to invoke privileged communication defenses. The law requires priests to report suspected abuse even when learned through the Sacrament of Confession.
On June 5, 2025, the plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction to prevent SB 5375 from taking effect as applied to confessional communications.

On July 18, 2025, Judge David G. Estudillo of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington granted the preliminary injunction, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on their Free Exercise claim.

The injunction prohibits enforcement of SB 5375 regarding the Sacrament of Confession against all Roman Catholic priests in Washington who fall under the administration of the three bishop plaintiffs.
During the litigation, all county prosecutor defendants agreed not to oppose the preliminary injunction and to be bound by it in exchange for a stay of proceedings against them.

On June 23, 2025, the United States moved to intervene on June 23, 2025, asserting that SB 5375 violates equal protection by infringing on fundamental religious rights and discriminating based on religion.
The intervention was granted on July 15, 2025.

evidence: On June 9, 2025, the Governor of California and the State of California, represented by the California Attorney General's office, filed suit against President Donald Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, and the U.S. Department of Defense, challenging the federalization of California's National Guard.

The case arose from immigration enforcement actions that began on June 6, 2025, when ICE conducted raids at multiple locations in Los Angeles County, including Home Depot stores, a donut shop, and a clothing wholesaler.

The raids, which resulted in 70-80 people detained and 44 arrested, sparked protests that included both peaceful demonstrations and incidents of violence, with some protesters throwing objects at federal officers, damaging federal property, and setting fires.

On June 7, 2025, President Trump invoked 10 U.S.C. § 12406 to federalize the California National Guard, asserting that protests constituted "a form of rebellion against the authority of the Government of the United States."

Secretary Hegseth issued orders calling 2,000 California National Guard members into federal service for 60 days, followed by an additional 2,000 members on June 9, along with deployment of 700 Marines from Camp Pendleton.
The orders were sent to California's Adjutant General rather than directly through Governor Newsom, who learned of the federalization only after it occurred and had not consented to it.

The plaintiffs brought ultra vires claims alleging that the federalization exceeded statutory authority because none of the three conditions required under § 12406 were met (foreign invasion, rebellion, or inability to execute laws with regular forces) and because the orders were not "issued through the governors of the States" as the statute requires.

They also alleged violations of the Tenth Amendment, arguing the federalization infringed on state sovereignty and police powers, and raised concerns about violations of the Posse Comitatus Act if military forces engaged in civilian law enforcement.

Throughout the proceedings, state and local law enforcement maintained they had sufficient resources to handle the protests, having made over 560 arrests, while the federal government argued that significant violence against federal officers and property damage justified the military deployment.

evidence: On March 25, 2025, two labor unions representing faculty and academic professionals—the American Association of University Professors and the American Federation of Teachers—filed suit challenging the termination of approximately $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University.
The case arose after President Trump issued an executive order on January 29, 2025, directing agencies to combat antisemitism on college campuses.

Following reports of antisemitic incidents at Columbia since October 2023, including the occupation of Hamilton Hall and establishment of protest encampments, federal agencies began reviewing Columbia's compliance with civil rights obligations.

On March 7, 2025, the agencies announced the immediate cancellation of approximately $400 million in grants and contracts to Columbia, citing the university's 'continued inaction in the face of persistent harassment of Jewish students.'

The agencies terminated grants pursuant to regulatory provisions allowing termination when awards 'no longer effectuate program goals or agency priorities' and contracts for 'convenience of the Government,' rather than through Title VI enforcement procedures.

On March 13, 2025, federal officials sent Columbia a letter outlining nine demands as 'preconditions' for any continued federal funding relationship, including requirements to expel certain students, abolish the University Judicial Board, ban masks intended to conceal identity, place the Middle East, South Asian, and African Studies department under 'academic receivership,' and reform admissions practices.
Columbia responded on March 21 by announcing eighteen reforms, many of which it had been developing for months before receiving the federal demands.

The plaintiff unions brought ten claims under the First Amendment, Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause, Tenth Amendment, Spending Clause, Administrative Procedure Act, separation of powers doctrine, and unconstitutional conditions doctrine.
They argued that the government violated Title VI's procedural requirements for terminating funding and unconstitutionally coerced Columbia to suppress protected speech and academic freedom.

The government countered that it terminated funding pursuant to its discretionary authority under grant terms and regulations, not Title VI, and that plaintiffs lacked standing because they were neither parties to the grants nor intended beneficiaries.

After briefing on the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction filed April 3, 2025, Judge Mary Kay Vyskocil of the Southern District of New York issued an opinion on June 16, 2025, denying the motion and dismissing the case without prejudice for lack of standing.

The court found that the plaintiff unions failed to establish either organizational or representational standing, noting that the grants were awarded to Columbia, not to plaintiffs or their members, and that any injuries to faculty members were not fairly traceable to defendants' actions given Columbia's independent decision-making.
The court observed that Columbia itself had not challenged the funding terminations and was instead negotiating with the government.

The court also noted that the Supreme Court's recent decision in Department of Education v. California suggested that challenges to grant terminations belong in the Court of Federal Claims as contract claims rather than in district court.
The plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal on June 16, 2025.

Federal agencies canceled the funding on March 7, 2025 citing persistent harassment of Jewish students and terminated grants under regulatory provisions rather than Title VI. In March 13, 2025, the agencies sent a letter of nine demands as preconditions for continued funding; Columbia responded on March 21 with eighteen reforms. The unions filed ten claims alleging violations of the First Amendment, Fifth Amendment Due Process, Tenth Amendment, Spending Clause, Administrative Procedure Act, separation of powers, and unconstitutional conditions doctrines, while the government argued it had discretionary authority and that the unions lacked standing. Judge Mary Kay Vyskocil dismissed the case on June 16, 2025 for lack of standing, noting the grants were awarded to Columbia, not the unions, and citing Supreme Court guidance that such challenges belong in the Court of Federal Claims rather than district court. The plaintiffs appealed on June 16, 2025. The case highlights tensions between academic freedom and anti‑antisemitism efforts and raises standing and forum questions.

evidence: On May 7, 2025, seventeen states and the District of Columbia filed suit against the U.S. Department of Transportation and Federal Highway Administration challenging the agencies' freeze of $5 billion in congressionally appropriated funds for electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

Congress had established the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program through the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, appropriating $5 billion to be distributed to states between 2022 and 2026 according to a mandatory formula for building EV charging infrastructure. The statute required FHWA to issue guidance and states to submit deployment plans, which FHWA had approved for all plaintiff states for fiscal years 2022-2025.
On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14,154 directing all agencies to 'immediately pause the disbursement of funds' from the Infrastructure Act, including NEVI funds.

On February 6, 2025, FHWA implemented this directive by rescinding all NEVI guidance, revoking all previously approved state deployment plans, and prohibiting any new obligations of the approximately $2.74 billion in unobligated NEVI funds.

The plaintiff states alleged violations of the APA for exceeding statutory authority, arbitrary and capricious action, and failure to follow required procedures. They also raised constitutional claims under the separation of powers doctrine and Take Care Clause, arguing that the Executive Branch had improperly seized Congress's spending power. The states demonstrated concrete harms including canceled projects, withdrawn contractors, lost site agreements, budget disruptions, and reassignment of staff.

Judge Tana Lin heard oral argument on June 17, 2025, and issued a detailed order on June 24, 2025. The court found that defendants likely exceeded their statutory authority, as the Infrastructure Act mandated distribution of NEVI funds and provided only limited circumstances for withholding funds, none of which applied. The court also found the agency action arbitrary and capricious for failing to provide reasoned explanation or consider reliance interests, and determined that defendants violated separation of powers by refusing to spend congressionally appropriated funds based on policy disagreements.

The court granted the preliminary injunction for fourteen states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, and Wisconsin), ordering defendants to restore their state plans and cease withholding NEVI funds. The injunction was denied for the District of Columbia, Minnesota, and Vermont because they failed to submit declarations demonstrating irreparable harm.

evidence: Eight students at Columbia University and Barnard College filed this First Amendment lawsuit on March 13, 2025, challenging what they characterize as a government campaign to suppress pro-Palestine speech on campus through unconstitutional 'jawboning' - the practice of government officials coercing private parties to punish or suppress disfavored views.
The lawsuit stems from events following the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel.
The House Committee began investigating antisemitism on college campuses in February 2024, requesting extensive documents from Columbia and holding high-profile hearings.
During an April 17, 2024 hearing, then-Columbia President Minouche Shafik testified before the Committee and promised to crack down on demonstrations the Committee deemed antisemitic.
The next day, she called in the NYPD to clear a student encampment, resulting in 108 arrests.
Two weeks later, protesters occupied Hamilton Hall, allegedly taking two janitors hostage and causing property damage.

The Committee issued subpoenas to Columbia in August 2024, and on October 31, 2024, released a 325-page report that, despite redacting names, included enough detail about disciplinary cases that students could be identified.
The immediate catalyst for this lawsuit was the Committee's February 13, 2025 letter requesting all disciplinary records related to eleven specific campus incidents.
On March 3, 2025, federal agencies announced they were reviewing Columbia's $5 billion in federal funding for Title VI compliance.
On March 7, the administration announced it had 'canceled ~$400M in federal grants' to Columbia.

evidence: On May 5, 2025, nineteen states, the District of Columbia, and the People of the State of Michigan filed suit against Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and other HHS officials challenging a sweeping agency reorganization.

The case arose from HHS's March 27, 2025 announcement that it would terminate 10,000 employees, consolidate twenty-eight divisions into fifteen, close half of its regional offices, and create a new Administration for a Healthy America as part of Secretary Kennedy's "Make America Healthy Again" initiative.
The announcement followed President Trump's Executive Order 14210 directing large-scale reductions in force across federal agencies.

The states, represented by their attorneys general, alleged that the reorganization violated the Administrative Procedure Act as both arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, violated constitutional separation of powers and appropriations principles, and exceeded the agency's statutory authority.
They argued that HHS cannot unilaterally dismantle congressionally-created programs and refuse to spend appropriated funds.

The complaint detailed how the mass terminations would cripple statutorily-mandated functions at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, including infectious disease laboratories, occupational safety research, maternal health surveillance, and tobacco prevention programs.

On April 1, 2025, HHS sent termination notices placing 10,000 employees on immediate administrative leave with final termination scheduled for June 2, 2025, immediately locking them out of email accounts, laptops, and offices.

Secretary Kennedy publicly acknowledged that the reorganization was deliberately hasty, admitting he expected twenty percent of the terminations to be mistakes but chose not to conduct careful review because it would "take too long" and cause loss of "political momentum." He later testified to Congress that "decisive action quickly" was more important than accuracy.
The states documented immediate harms including shuttered CDC laboratories, offline data systems, halted grant processing, and loss of technical assistance for critical public health programs.
On May 9, 2025, the states moved for a preliminary injunction targeting specific agencies within HHS.
After expedited briefing and a May 20 hearing, District Judge Melissa R. DuBose granted the preliminary injunction on July 1, 2025.

The court rejected HHS's jurisdictional challenges, finding the states had standing based on concrete injuries, that the Civil Service Reform Act did not require channeling claims through administrative forums, and that the Tucker Act did not require filing in the Court of Federal Claims.

On the merits, the court found the March 27 announcement constituted reviewable final agency action that was both arbitrary and capricious—lacking any rational basis or cost-benefit analysis—and contrary to numerous statutes requiring HHS to maintain specific programs and spend appropriated funds.

The court enjoined HHS from implementing the planned terminations and reorganization at the CDC, FDA's Center for Tobacco Products, Office of Head Start, and Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation.
The court's order prohibited executing existing termination notices, issuing new ones, or placing additional employees on administrative leave at the specified agencies.
The court imposed only a nominal $100 bond.
On August 12, 2025, the court clarified the injunction's scope, specifying the particular CDC components and programs covered.
Defendants filed a notice of appeal the same day, with the case assigned number 25-1780 in the First Circuit.

Related litigation challenging similar reorganizations at other federal agencies was proceeding simultaneously in multiple federal courts, with some courts granting and others denying preliminary relief.
The case remains pending with briefing on defendants' motion to dismiss scheduled through September 2025.

The complaint details how the mass terminations would cripple CDC functions, including infectious disease laboratories, occupational safety research, maternal health surveillance, and tobacco prevention programs; termination notices were issued on April 1, 2025, placing employees on immediate administrative leave and locking them out of email, laptops, and offices. evidence: On April 29, 2025, twenty-four states and the District of Columbia filed suit against the Corporation for National and Community Service (operating as AmeriCorps) and its Interim Agency Head Jennifer Bastress Tahmasebi, alleging violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the Constitution's separation of powers doctrine, and statutory requirements. The plaintiffs are represented by their respective attorneys general. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland and assigned to Judge Deborah L. Boardman.

The lawsuit arose from AmeriCorps's sweeping actions in April 2025 to dismantle the federal agency for national service and volunteerism. Following consultations with the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) team to implement Executive Order 14222, AmeriCorps placed approximately 85 percent of its 720-person staff on administrative leave on April 16, 2025, and subsequently reduced its workforce to 116 employees through reductions in force. On April 15, 2025, the agency ordered all members of the National Civilian Community Corps—a residential volunteer program for young adults to leave their service posts pending termination from the program. Most significantly, on April 25, 2025, AmeriCorps terminated 1,031 grant-funded programs across the country, representing nearly $400 million in federal funding and affecting approximately 30,000 AmeriCorps members, VISTA members, and AmeriCorps Seniors volunteers. The termination letters stated simply that "the award no longer effectuates agency priorities."

The plaintiffs alleged these actions violated the APA in multiple ways: by failing to engage in required notice-and-comment rulemaking, acting arbitrarily and capriciously, and acting contrary to law. Specifically, they argued AmeriCorps violated a provision in the 2024 and 2025 appropriations acts requiring that the agency "make any significant changes to program requirements, service delivery or policy only through public notice and comment rulemaking." They also raised constitutional separation of powers claims and argued the actions exceeded the agency's statutory authority.

On May 6, 2025, the states moved for a preliminary injunction. Following briefing and a hearing on May 19, 2025, Judge Boardman issued a memorandum opinion and order on June 5, 2025, granting the preliminary injunction in part. The court found that the mass closure of AmeriCorps programs and removal of NCCC members constituted "significant changes to service delivery" that required notice-and-comment rulemaking under the appropriations acts. The court ordered AmeriCorps to restore the affected programs in the plaintiff states by reinstating the terminated grants and returning AmeriCorps and VISTA members to service if they were willing and able to return. The court also ordered the restoration of NCCC members nationwide. However, the court denied the request to enjoin the staff reductions, finding the states lacked standing to challenge those personnel decisions.

On July 10, 2025, the court modified the preliminary injunction in response to the Supreme Court's June 27, 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, which held that federal courts lack authority to issue universal injunctions. The modification limited the notice-and-comment requirement to changes that harm the plaintiff states. The preliminary injunction remains in effect until further order of the court, with the plaintiffs having posted a nominal bond of $100 per state.

The terminated programs had provided critical services including disaster relief, veterans support, education assistance, environmental conservation, and public health initiatives. Many programs served vulnerable populations such as children with disabilities, seniors, and communities recovering from natural disasters. The court found the states would suffer irreparable harm from the loss of these services and the diversion of state resources needed to fill the gaps left by the federal program terminations.

The plaintiffs alleged these actions violated the APA by failing notice‑and‑comment rulemaking, acting arbitrarily, capriciously, and contrary to law, and exceeded the agency's statutory authority. evidence: On June 27, 2025, two environmental organizations—Friends of the Everglades and the Center for Biological Diversity—filed suit in the Southern District of Florida challenging the construction of a mass immigration detention facility at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport (TNT) in the Big Cypress National Preserve.

The case arose after FDEM took control of the TNT site on June 23, 2025, pursuant to Governor DeSantis's emergency powers related to illegal immigration, and immediately began constructing what officials called 'Alligator Alcatraz'—a temporary detention facility designed to house up to 5,000 immigration detainees.

The TNT site sits within the Big Cypress National Preserve, an environmentally sensitive wetland ecosystem that serves as habitat for several endangered and threatened species, including the Florida panther, Florida bonneted bat, Everglade snail kite, and wood stork.
Construction proceeded rapidly without any environmental impact statement or environmental assessment as required under NEPA for major federal actions significantly affecting the human environment.

After extensive briefing and a four-day evidentiary hearing from August 6-13, 2025, Judge Williams granted a temporary restraining order on August 7, 2025, prohibiting further construction activities including installation of additional lighting, paving, fencing, or placement of additional structures.

On August 21, 2025, the court issued a comprehensive preliminary injunction that immediately prohibited bringing new detainees to the facility, ceased all new construction, and required removal of recently installed infrastructure including fencing, lighting, generators, and waste management systems within sixty days.

The court found that NEPA applied based on evidence of substantial federal control and involvement, including federal funding commitments of $450-600 million annually through FEMA's Detention Support Grant Program, ICE's supervision of immigration enforcement activities at the facility through 287(g) agreements with multiple Florida law enforcement agencies, and statements by state officials that the facility was requested and would be fully funded by the federal government.

The court also ruled that venue was proper in the Southern District of Florida, finding that substantial events giving rise to the claims occurred there, including Miami-Dade County's ownership of the property, ICE Miami field office's supervision of detention operations, and environmental impacts affecting the Miccosukee Tribe's lands in Miami-Dade County.

The court concluded that the plaintiffs demonstrated irreparable harm through loss of procedural rights under NEPA, habitat destruction affecting endangered species, light and noise pollution impacting their use and enjoyment of the preserve, and potential contamination of wetlands from inadequate stormwater management at the rapidly constructed facility.
The facility had been operational since July 1, 2025, housing hundreds of detainees to alleviate overcrowding at other facilities before the preliminary injunction effectively ordered its closure.
extracted.value: The case involves Friends of the Everglades and the Center for Biological Diversity filing suit on June 27, 2025, challenging the construction of a mass immigration detention facility at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport in the Big Cypress National Preserve. The facility was begun by Florida Division of Emergency Management on June 23, 2025, as a temporary detention center called Alligator Alcatraz, designed to house up to 5,000 detainees. The site lies within an environmentally sensitive wetland that hosts endangered species such as the Florida panther. Construction proceeded without an environmental impact statement or assessment required by NEPA. Evidence includes the court’s temporary restraining order issued August 7, 2025 and the preliminary injunction issued August 21, 2025, halting construction and further detainee intake. Background information includes federal funding commitments of $450‑$600 million annually via FEMA’s Detention Support Grant Program, ICE supervision through 287(g) agreements, and statements that the facility was federally funded, establishing NEPA applicability. The court found irreparable harm from loss of procedural rights, habitat destruction, light and noise pollution, and potential wetland contamination.

evidence: On April 11, 2025, two faculty associations—the American Association of University Professors-Harvard Faculty Chapter and the national AAUP, later joined by the International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW)—filed suit in federal district court against multiple federal agencies and their heads.

The plaintiffs, represented by private law firms Selendy Gay PLLC and Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll PLLC, challenged the Trump administration's threats to withdraw and ultimate termination of billions of dollars in federal research funding from Harvard University.

After creating a multi-agency Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism in February 2025, defendants announced on March 31, 2025 that they were reviewing Harvard's federal funding for alleged failures to address antisemitism.

Three days later, on April 3, defendants sent Harvard a letter demanding sweeping reforms including eliminating all 'DEI programs,' implementing 'viewpoint diversity' audits of faculty, instituting mask bans, centralizing student discipline, and overhauling admissions and hiring practices.

An April 11 letter expanded these demands further, requiring Harvard to report foreign students who commit conduct violations to immigration authorities and to reform specific academic departments the administration deemed problematic.
When Harvard rejected these demands through counsel on April 14, the administration immediately froze over $2 billion in federal funding.
Between May 6 and May 12, 2025, various federal agencies formally terminated approximately $2.7 billion in grants to Harvard.

The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and the First Amendment. They alleged defendants violated the APA by failing to follow Title VI of the Civil Rights Act's mandatory procedures for terminating federal funding based on civil rights violations.

Title VI requires agencies to make specific findings of noncompliance, attempt voluntary resolution, provide notice and opportunity for a hearing, and report to Congress thirty days before any funding termination becomes effective—none of which occurred here.

The administrative record revealed no actual investigation of antisemitism at Harvard. Instead, defendants relied on a politically motivated House report and various unsubstantiated allegations while ignoring Harvard's existing efforts to combat antisemitism, including its January 2025 settlement of two Title VI lawsuits where it agreed to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism and implement various reforms.

Public statements by President Trump and defendant Leo Terrell made clear the political motivation, with Trump calling Harvard 'a threat to Democracy' that 'teaches Hate and Stupidity' and Terrell stating the goal was to 'bankrupt these universities' because 'the academic system in this country has been hijacked by the left.'

The funding terminations immediately harmed plaintiffs' members by forcing cessation of ongoing research, including clinical trials, causing layoffs of research staff, preventing graduate students from completing degrees, and creating a climate of fear and self-censorship among faculty.

Multiple Harvard faculty members submitted declarations detailing how the funding cuts forced them to halt multi-year studies, lay off trained personnel, and abandon research partnerships, with some describing the damage as potentially career-ending.
The plaintiffs sought declaratory and injunctive relief to restore funding and prevent similar future actions without compliance with legal procedures.

The case was assigned to Judge Allison D. Burroughs and proceeded on an expedited schedule, with the plaintiffs filing for summary judgment on June 2, 2025, supported by amicus briefs from organizations including A Jewish Voice for Peace and Public Citizen.

extracted.value: The case involves five nonprofit organizations filing a class action lawsuit on May 21, 2025, challenging the Department of Justice Office of Justice Programs' abrupt termination in April 2025 of over 370 multi-year grants totaling more than $820 million; the terminations were communicated via identical notices that offered no individualized explanations and ordered recipients to stop work immediately; the DOJ claimed it had changed priorities to focus on law enforcement and victim services, yet the terminated grants served those same purposes; plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act alleging arbitrary and capricious terminations, as well as constitutional violations—including denial of due process, void for vagueness, separation of powers, and Take Care Clause violations—and an equitable ultra vires claim against the Attorney General and OJP's acting head, seeking declaratory judgment and injunctive relief including grant reinstatement; the court denied the preliminary injunction, granted the motion to dismiss, and denied class certification, finding the claims essentially contractual and lacking jurisdiction and that the constitutional claims failed on their merits; the terminations caused staff layoffs, program closures, and harmed vulnerable communities, prompting amicus briefs from eighteen states and the District of Columbia; the plaintiffs were Vera Institute of Justice, Center for Children & Youth Justice, Chinese for Affinitive Action (doing business as Stop AAPI Hate), FORCE Detroit, and Health Resources in Action, with Democracy Forward Foundation and Perry Law as private counsel.
evidence: On May 21, 2025, five nonprofit organizations filed a class action lawsuit challenging the Department of Justice Office of Justice Programs' abrupt termination of over 370 multi-year grants totaling more than $820 million.

In April 2025, OJP had sent identical termination notices to grant recipients, including the five plaintiff organizations, stating only that the awards 'no longer effectuate[] the program goals or agency priorities' pursuant to 2 C.F.R. § 200.340(a)(4).
The notices offered no individualized explanations and ordered recipients to stop work immediately.

The Department claimed it had 'changed its priorities' to focus on 'more directly supporting certain law enforcement operations, combatting violent crime, protecting American children, and supporting American victims of trafficking and sexual assault,' yet the terminated grants served these exact purposes—funding violence intervention programs, victim services, law enforcement training, and community safety initiatives.
The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging the terminations were arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.

The plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction and class certification. The defendants, represented by the Department of Justice, opposed these motions and moved to dismiss, arguing primarily that the court lacked jurisdiction because the claims were essentially contractual and belonged in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act.

A hearing before Judge Amit P. Mehta on June 26, 2025, revealed the government's inability to explain the terminations—when pressed, DOJ's counsel could not articulate why any individual grant was terminated as inconsistent with the agency's priorities, despite those grants directly serving the stated priorities.
On July 7, 2025, Judge Mehta denied the preliminary injunction, granted the defendants' motion to dismiss, and denied the class certification motion as moot.

The court found OJP's terminations 'unquestionably arbitrary, at least in lay terms' and called the government's conduct 'shameful,' but concluded it lacked jurisdiction over the APA claims, finding them essentially contractual in nature. The court held that under Department of Education v. California, 145 S. Ct. 966 (2025), such claims belonged exclusively in the Court of Federal Claims.

evidence: On April 11, 2025, the law firm Susman Godfrey LLP filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging Executive Order 14,263 issued by President Donald Trump on April 9, 2025.
The Executive Order, titled 'Addressing Risks from Susman Godfrey,' targeted the firm based on its representation of clients and causes that President Trump opposed.

The Order imposed severe restrictions on Susman Godfrey, including immediate suspension of all security clearances held by firm personnel, requirements that government contractors disclose any business with the firm and potentially face contract termination, limitations on access to federal buildings and engagement with federal employees, and restrictions on federal hiring of Susman employees.

Susman challenged the Order on multiple constitutional grounds, alleging violations of the First Amendment (retaliation for protected speech, viewpoint discrimination, interference with petition rights and freedom of association), the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause (deprivation of liberty and property interests without process, vagueness, and violation of clients' right to counsel), equal protection, and separation of powers principles.

The court permanently enjoined the Executive Order in its entirety, declaring it 'unconstitutional and therefore null and void.'
President Trump had previously issued orders against Perkins Coie LLP, Jenner & Block LLP, and Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale & Dorr LLP, all of which were enjoined by federal courts.
